newsitem.title: INDIA: Fog hangs over India's oil price strategy.
newsitem.headline: Fog hangs over India's oil price strategy.

text.p: India is keeping its options open on how to clear a multi-billion dollar backlog of repayments due to domestic oil companies and on which petroleum product prices to raise, a government spokesman said on Friday.

United News of India (UNI) quoted the spokesman as saying: "The Prime Minister had conveyed that several alternatives to bridge the gap were under study. The issue regarding the large deficit of nearly 190 ($5.3 billion) billion rupees that keeps increasing, needs attention."

UNI also quoted the spokesman as saying the federal government would soon take a decision on a petroleum products price hike after consultations with the United Front government's policy-setting steering committee.

Oil companies are owed the money for selling refined product below market prices to support India's subsidy regime, but the debt to the companies ballooned when world oil prices surged late last year and India left its domestic prices unchanged.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral in a television interview on Thursday appeared to say a decision was close at hand, and drastic cuts in subsidies on diesel and liquefied petroleun gas (LPG) would be made.
But the spokesman clarified that while Gujral said a price increase in some products appeared unavoidable the question of which consumers needed to be subsidised was still undecided.
Gujral, in the interview, also raised the possibility that the government might be ready to wipe out the debt to companies and take the deficit onto its own books.
Currently the oil companies sell some products at a loss, their losses are tallied in the oil pool account and they wait to be reimbursed from the pool by the Oil Coordination Committee (OCC).
But, while the OCC is government controlled, the oil pool account is separate from the fiscal deficit.
Consolidating the oil pool into the fiscal deficit, along with reductions in subsidies, would remove a massive obstacle to deregulation of India's oil sector.
"If they are able to all this, one of the biggest impediments to de-control will be removed," one oil sector analyst, with a foreign stockbrokerage in Bombay, commented.
But Gujral gave few hints how he would do the job.
"We will find a way out. And this is what we are trying to build a concensus on. Let me hope I will succeed," he said.
But until the steering committee finally meets to decide, analysts could only speculate.
"Everything is up in the air until the next steering committee meeting," P. Dhileepan, oil analyst at NatWest Markets in Bombay, told Reuters.
That meeting has been deferred three times so far, after two inconclusive earlier meetings.
There is no confirmation of a new date, and official sources said a core group of key decision-makers may meet on July 17 and the steering committee would meet soon after.
Urgent action is needed. Oil refiners are facing a credit crunch, and have told the government that unless it stumps up money soon there will be no cash in their kitty to buy crude.
New Petroleum Minister Janeshwar Mishra drove the point home on Thursday. "Under the present circumstances, imports may dry up," he said.
Indian Oil Corp, the country's sole importing agency, has already borrowed 140 billion rupees ($3.9 billion) and is owed 90 billion from the oil pool. ($1=35.7 rupees)
